First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y+3x & =-6 \\ 2y & =-3x-6 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}x-3\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/715e1292edaf78979f6b9ae36586a8196dcc30e865915e7eefba2360281f85ec.png)

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{3}{2}x-3$ and passes through the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$

The given line has a slope of $-\frac{3}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{2}{3}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{2}{3}(x-2) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{4}{3} \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{3}{2}x-3 \\ y=\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}x-3 & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{5}{6} \\ -\frac{3}{2}x-\frac{2}{3}x & =-\frac{5}{6}+3 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =\frac{13}{6} \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into either of the two equations gives $y=-\frac{3}{2}.$ So, our solution is $x=-1$ and $y=-\frac{3}{2}.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(-1,-\frac{3}{2}).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,-\frac{3}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-1-2)}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ and the line $2y+3x=-6$ is $\sqrt{13}.$
